text: Rain, a street lamp, and the Kennington Road. Somewhere out there, most of the Metropolitan Police.
Cod, haddock, plaice, skate, saveloy. No regret. Regret must be off.
The door, the rain, and somewhere down the Kennington Road, a goose in a police helmet.
The door, and the rain, and the goose. The goose wants chips. The goose always wants chips.
Out there it's raining, and my face is on every newspaper in London. In here there are chips.
Private, that is. Staff only.
Cod in batter the size of a canoe, and a hill of chips. I haven't eaten since Zürich.
Paying for that, are we?
Do you take Swiss francs?
Do I look Swiss?
The snooker. Nobody in England has ever been arrested during the snooker.
That's me, in the photograph from my pass. WANTED: JACK HARROW. TRAITOR. WITH GOOSE. They've got the goose's good side.
Pickled eggs, floating in a jar like evidence. Nobody has bought one since 1974. They're the same eggs.
A spike of chip orders. And in the middle of them, spiked straight through the word SECRET, a memo from Headquarters.
Stan has been using the most secret piece of paper south of the river as a chip order.
PC Dobbs's helmet, upside down on the counter beside his chips, like a collection plate.
Not while he keeps looking my way. He looks at me, then at the television, then at me.
He didn't even blink. It's the final frame.
The goose, out in the rain, with her beak pressed to the glass, glaring at PC Dobbs's chips.
Not now, Colonel. Wait there. Look innocent.
PC Dobbs of Kennington Road: six foot two of Metropolitan Police, eating chips out of the Evening Post. My face is on the front of the Evening Post.
Stan Pike: forty years behind this counter, thirty of them for the Service. Stan never asks questions. Stan never answers them, either.
Here, Stan. Turn it up. It's that traitor again.
Can't reach, can I? Got my hands full of haddock.
That's me on the television. And that's a policeman, three feet from it. I'd rather they didn't meet.
Shh. He's on the pink.
Evening, sir. Shocking weather. Here, don't I know you from somewhere?
I've got one of those faces.
No, I'm sure of it. It'll come to me.
Not if I can help it.
I'll leave it on the snooker. For everyone's sake.
Oi! I was watching that.
It's the final frame, Constable.
Is it? Is it the final frame? Ooh.
Look at that. Look at the angle on that.
A whole nation, frozen in front of a green table. I could walk off with anything.
There. Now you look like the law.
Here. That goose has got my helmet.
That's the goose off the telly, that is.
The traitor's goose! OI! You stop right there, in the name of the law!
He'll never catch her. She's done this before.
Van leaves at seven sharp. Kip on the sofa upstairs. Mind the cat, he bites.
Not now, sunshine. There's a copper in the shop, and your face is on the telly behind him.
Evening. What'll it be?
Cod and chips twice, hold the vinegar.
That's the old one, that is. They changed it in March. Memo went round.
A memo. Stan never throws anything away. He just puts it on a spike.
Stan, it's me. Jack.
Never seen you before in my life, sir. What'll it be?
Thirty years in the Service. Stan does everything by the book.
Just chips, please.
Forty-five pence.
Haddock, no batter, and a side of regret.
Right you are, sir. One haddock, no batter, side of regret.
Hello, Jack. You look terrible.
I've been on a fishing boat for two days with a goose.
Madame Novak was in on Tuesday. Left you this.

"Jack. Rupert is having tea with me and the Minister at the Wellington, four o'clock on Thursday. The Minister is an old friend, and a fool, but an honest one. Bring him something he can hold. Love, Z. P.S. Feed the goose."
Something the Minister can hold. The proof is in Control's office, on the fourth floor of Headquarters, where every guard has my photograph.
Every guard's got your photograph, sunshine. No guard's got a clue. The canteen buys its fish off me: goods yard, half past seven, every morning. Kippers for the Director.
Van leaves at seven. Here's my spare coat, and the delivery note. Don't lose the note. Grimes on the gate can't read, but he likes to hold it.
Stan, you're a genius.
I know. Nobody ever asks.
Morning! Deliveries this way. Everything through me. That's the rules.
Sergeant Grimes, on the gate. He's been on that gate since the Suez Crisis. He saw me every day for eleven years.
The Houses of Parliament, across the river in the rain. Somewhere in there is a Minister who is about to have a very difficult tea.
Headquarters: twenty storeys of grey concrete with no name on the door, which is how everyone in London knows exactly what it is.
A barrier, a sentry box and Sergeant Grimes: the Service's first line of defence. Mostly against fish.
Stan's van: THE PLAICE TO BE, FRESH FISH DAILY. Forty kippers in the back, and a goose in the front.
Nothing else back there but the smell.
Forty kippers and a stone of cod. The kippers are looking at me.
The goose, in the driver's seat, watching Sergeant Grimes the way she watches a sandwich.
Is that a goose in your van?
It's a kipper. A big one.
Blimey.
Oi! Not so fast, sunshine. Deliveries through me. That's the rules.
Sergeant Grimes: a waxed moustache, a chest full of medals, and a memory like a colander. Every morning for eleven years he said "Morning, Mr Harrow."
I don't want your fish, son. I want your note. That's the rules.
Goods lift, fourth floor, canteen's on the left. Don't touch anything, it's all secret.
Fish, is it? Where's the fish, then? You can't deliver fish without fish. That's the rules.
Delivery note. No note, no entry. That's the rules.
A note for fish, and no fish? That's not the rules.
Let's have a look.
Forty... kippers... for the Director. One stone of cod, canteen. Signed, S. Pike. Where's Stan, then?
Stan's got his feet up. I'm his nephew, Kevin.
Kevin! He never said he had a nephew.
Stan's at the dentist.
Stan? At the dentist? Stan's never been to a dentist in his life. You can tell.
Stan's been arrested for treason.
Stan! Treason! Ha! That's a good one.
Here. Has anyone ever told you, you look just like that traitor? Off the telly?
I get it all the time. Terrible for business.
I bet it is. Poor sod.
The traitor's much better looking.
He is, and all. No offence.
Do I? Which traitor?
Good point. We get a lot of them, in this building.
Mr Harrow. You smell of haddock.
Kippers, Miss Penrose. Forty of them.
I never believed a word of it, you know. You always brought me back chocolates. Traitors don't bring back chocolates.
Is he in?
Since six. He never leaves that office before nine. Not for fire drills, not for the Director, not for the Queen. He had the Queen on hold once.
PENROSE. Where is my tea?
Coming, sir!
He's having tea with his mother at four, at the Wellington, with the Minister. Jacket and tie, at the Wellington. They turned away a duke last Christmas for wearing a cravat.
WALLS HAVE EARS. CANTEEN: KIPPERS FRIDAY. LOST: ONE UMBRELLA, CONTROL'S. DO NOT ASK HIM ABOUT IT.
IN CASE OF FIRE, BREAK GLASS. The last time somebody did, Control stayed at his desk and the rest of the building stood in the rain for an hour.
Tempting. Very tempting. But he'd just stay at his desk.
Four drawers each, all marked SECRET. The top one is marked BISCUITS.
Locked. Even the biscuits.
The goods lift, back down to Grimes and the rain.
Not without what I came for.
He's in there. I can hear him stirring his tea. Nobody stirs tea that angrily.
An air vent, low on the wall. It runs straight through into Control's office. I can hear him humming Elgar through it.
I could put something in it. Something Control would rather not smell.
Miss Penrose: thirty years outside Control's door, a hundred and twenty words a minute, and the only person in this building who has never been fooled by anybody.
Hurry, Mr Harrow. The Director's kettle isn't that long.
He's gone up to the Director, on the ninth floor. He'll be twenty minutes. The Director has a very long kettle.
His desk will be locked.
Yes. It will.
I have a spare key, for when he locks himself out. Which is twice a week. It is in my top drawer, and I am going to powder my nose.
Thank you, Miss Penrose.
For what? I'm powdering my nose.
Could you get him out of there?
I can't lie to Control, Mr Harrow. I go red. I went red at my own wedding, and I meant every word.
Doesn't anything make him leave?
Smells. He has a very delicate nose. Last year the canteen boiled a cabbage, and he worked from his club for a week.
A delicate nose. And I have forty kippers.
Mind the lift, Mr Harrow. It sticks on three.
Once was enough. For the kipper, anyway.
One kipper, into the vent. I'm sorry, kipper. You died for your country, and now you're doing it again.
Penrose. PENROSE. What is that SMELL?
The fish man is delivering, sir.
It's in my office. It's in my TEA. I cannot think in this. I shall be with the Director.
You. Fish man.
Sir.
You smell of fish.
Occupational hazard, sir.
Hm.
Penrose, open every window in my office. And have the fish man shot.
Eleven years he's been my boss, and he's never once looked at a fishmonger.
Control's office. It smells of Lapsang Souchong, old leather and, now, very strongly, of kipper.
Rain on the river, and Parliament across it. From here Control can watch the Minister arrive for work, and decide how much to tell him.
The first Control, 1909. He also looks as though somebody has put a kipper in his air vent.
A map of Karvonia with pins in it: Karvograd, the Zlatá pass, the airbase. Every place somebody tried to kill me this year, in red.
A bowler hat and an umbrella. Control's famous lost umbrella. It was here the whole time.
Control's coat stand: a bowler, an umbrella, and a spare tie in the stripes of the Coldstream Guards.
I'll leave him the umbrella. I'm not a monster.
Jacket and tie at the Wellington, Miss Penrose said. I have a jacket. It's a fish jacket, but it's a jacket.
Control's teapot, in a knitted cosy of red, white and blue. His mother knitted it. It's the only thing in London he's never lied to.
Stone cold, stewed black, and now faintly of kipper.
The red telephone, straight through to the Minister. It has rung all week. He never answers it.
The drawer, empty now apart from a spoon.
A drawer with a brass lock. Control keeps his secrets the way he keeps his tea: locked up, and stewed.
Empty, apart from a spoon.
Locked.
Control's wastepaper basket. Screwed-up paper, a teabag and... my name?
A notepad, covered in my signature. Forty times. The first ones are terrible. By the bottom of the page, even I'd sign for them.
A paying-in book for account 44-771, Zürich. Every stub in Control's own small, tidy hand. Eighty million francs, a little at a time.
Something the Minister can hold, in his own handwriting. Now I just need something to wear to tea.
Penrose, I forgot my umbr...
HARROW.
Morning, sir. Kippers.
GUARDS! Guards, he's in my office! He's got my PAYING-IN BOOK! He's got my TIE!
Mind your tea, sir.
Good afternoon, sir. Welcome to the Wellington. Have you a reservation?
I'm with Madame Novak.
Of course you are, sir.
I'm afraid the Palm Court does require a jacket and tie, sir.
This is a jacket.
It is a fish jacket, sir.
A string trio, sawing through Elgar. The cellist has been asleep since Pomp and Circumstance.
Scones, clotted cream, and those little cakes that look like hats.
After the arrest, darling. Scones are for after.
A velvet rope, and on the far side of it, England.
Jacket and tie, sir. It is the rule. We turned away a duke last Christmas.
Mr Fothergill, the maître d': tailcoat, carnation, and a face that has been turning people away from tea since the Coronation.
We have our own kippers, sir. From Scotland. They are better dressed.
Zdenka Novak, in her furs, pouring tea for her son and the Minister as if nobody had ever been framed for treason. It is her favourite kind of tea party.
Madame Novak, at the best table, with the Minister and her son. She has seen me. She winked.
The Minister: Harrow and Oxford, the Garrick Club, and the jam. He is an honest man, Madame Novak says. A fool, but an honest one. That will have to do.
The Minister, buttering a scone, on the far side of a velvet rope.
Control, in his second-best suit, sipping Lapsang and not looking at me. His grey men are outside. He isn't worried. That worries me.
That is MY tie.
Control, at his mother's table. He saw me come in. He's smiling. That's never good.
A large man at the next table, reading the racing pages upside down. Special Branch, or a very confused bookmaker.
Not now, sir. I'm reading.
A jacket and tie, sir. I am sure sir has a tie somewhere about his person.
The bill for Madame Novak's table, please.
Madame Novak's tea is never billed, sir. It is a tradition. Since 1953.
Just this once. For the gentleman in grey.
...Very good, sir.
Enjoy your tea, sir.
Enjoy your tea, sir. The scones are warm, and the cream is Cornish.
The Coldstream Guards! I do beg your pardon, sir. A Guards tie covers a multitude of fish.
This way, sir. Madame Novak's table.
That is my tie.
It's a Guards tie, Rupert. You were in the Pay Corps.
Jack. When Rupert was six he took me to tea at the Ritz with his pocket money, and he signed the bill. He has signed every bill since, darling. He cannot bear to let anybody else pay.
It is his only generous quality.
He signs every bill. He's spent a year practising my signature. I wonder which one his hand remembers.
Show him, Jack. Something he can hold. Ministers like to hold things. It makes them feel they are in charge.
Jack, darling. You smell of the sea. Sit down, have a scone.
Rupert, don't make that face. It will stick.
Mother, he is a traitor, and he is wearing my tie.
He looks much nicer in it than you did.
Give it up, Harrow. The Minister believes what I tell him. He always has. It saves him reading.
Hello, Harrow. You've come a very long way to be arrested.
More proof, Harrow. Something I can hold, in black and white. Pass the cream.
Proof, Harrow. Something I can hold.
Harrow! Good Lord. Zdenka says you're innocent. Rupert says you're a traitor. I say, somebody pass the jam.
Minister, I can prove it.
Can you? Splendid. Proof I can hold, mind. I can't arrest a man on a feeling. I tried that once, and it was the Archbishop.
A paying-in book. Account four four, seven seven one. Rupert, this is your handwriting.
A forgery, Minister. Harrow is an accomplished forger. It is in his file.
Is it? Well. It's a jolly good forgery.
Harrow's signature. Forty times. Rather good by the end.
Harrow, practising his own signature, Minister. Vanity. It is in his file.
Hm. I can't arrest a man for a notepad, Zdenka. I'd have to arrest my wife.
Good Lord, no. Rupert always pays. Always has.
Kippers? At tea? Harrow, this is the Wellington.
It's my word against his, and he has the better tie. I need Rupert to sign something, here, in front of the Minister.
Your bill, sir.
Give me that. Nobody pays for Mother's tea but me.
There.
Eleven pounds forty, very reasonable, and signed...
"Jack Harrow."
Rupert. Why have you signed the bill "Jack Harrow"?
...Force of habit.
Oh, Rupert.
Inspector!
Rupert Novak, I am arresting you under the Official Secrets Act. You do not have to say anything.
Ha. Oh, Harrow. Ha ha ha.
You think this is the end? I was only ever the middleman. I moved the money. I signed the cheques. Your cheques.
Then who bought the aircraft?
Nobody bought them, Harrow. The buyer never needed to buy anything. You don't pay for aeroplanes when your own brother builds them.
Colonel Vasko has a sister.
Aunt Olga sends her regards. May Day in Moscow will be glorious this year. Twelve black aircraft over Red Square.
Not the goose. Mother, keep that goose away from me.
The goose remembers Aunt Olga. And I'm fairly sure Aunt Olga remembers the goose.
PC Dobbs is watching the news, and the news is about me. Something else on that television, quickly.
A police helmet, and a goose at the door. The goose has always wanted to be in the police.
He's glued to the snooker. And his helmet is sitting on the counter.
Stan does everything by the book. Give him the phrase from the memo.
Stan wants the recognition phrase, and they changed it in March. Stan keeps everything on that spike.
Upstairs, and some sleep.
A fish delivery needs fish. They're in the back of the van.
Grimes wants to hold the delivery note.
The goods lift, and up to the fourth floor.
Control has a delicate nose, and that vent goes straight into his office. And I have forty kippers.
Miss Penrose knows Control better than anyone. What makes him leave his office?
His desk will be locked. Miss Penrose might know something about that.
Control's office, while he's upstairs with the Director.
The desk drawer, and Miss Penrose's spare key.
Control's wastepaper basket. Nobody ever empties a spy's wastepaper basket properly.
Jacket and tie, at the Wellington. Control keeps a spare on his coat stand.
Jacket and tie, Mr Fothergill says. I have Control's spare tie.
Show the Minister the paying-in book, and the signature pad.
Control signs every bill, Madame Novak says. Mr Fothergill could bring one.
Give Control the bill, and let him sign it.
Nothing special.
That won't work.
I don't think so.
Not a chance.
That doesn't help here.
Those two don't go together.
Stop that man! He is a traitor! And he smells of FISH!
Mind the gap. Mind the gap. Mind the gap.
Sorry. Sorry. Terribly sorry. Excuse me. Sorry.
Stand clear of the closing doors, please.

The doors close on the grey men. The train pulls out. I ride it to the end of the line, and back, and to the end again, until four o'clock. Nobody on the Underground looks at anybody. It's the safest place in London.
A white coat, a flat cap, a Guards tie in my pocket and one kipper, for luck. Across the road a blue van pulls up, and something white gets out of it.
In the Swiss Alps, Jack stopped a cuckoo clock from opening Colonel Vasko's hangar, and found the account that paid for the Nightglass fleet. The name on the account was his own.

Franz drove through the night. A fishing boat did the rest. Jack comes ashore with no passport, no money and a goose, and at every station his face is on the front of the Evening Post: TRAITOR. Underneath, smaller: AND GOOSE.
A chip shop called The Plaice to Be, which for thirty years has been the Service's safe house south of the river. And tonight, a policeman eating chips at the counter.
Twelve black aircraft on the ice, in a row, under the northern lights. In a hut at the end of the runway, Aunt Olga is knitting something enormous.
The Minister has cleared Jack's name, paid the bill himself, and apologised to the goose. The goose has not accepted.
Aunt Olga.
Chapter Eleven: White Out.
PC Dobbs's helmet, still warm, with a chip stuck to the badge. I've stolen a lot of things for my country. This is the first one that's a hat.
HEADQUARTERS · SAFE HOUSES · SECRET. "From 1 March the recognition phrase at Lambeth is: Haddock, no batter, and a side of regret." There's a thumbprint of batter over the word SECRET.
THE PLAICE TO BE · DELIVERY NOTE. Headquarters canteen: forty kippers (for the Director), one stone of cod. Signed, S. Pike. There's a chip stuck to it.
Forty kippers for the Director's breakfast, and a stone of cod, in a wooden crate marked THE PLAICE TO BE. The kippers are looking at me.
The spare key to Control's desk, on a ring with a little brass teapot. "He locks himself out twice a week," says Miss Penrose. "It's the only time he says please."
A paying-in book for numbered account 44-771, in Zürich. Every stub filled in in Control's small, tidy hand. Eighty million francs, a little at a time.
A notepad from Control's wastepaper basket, covered in my signature, forty times. The first ones are terrible. By the bottom of the page, even I'd sign for them.
Control's spare tie, in the stripes of the Coldstream Guards. Control was never in the Coldstream Guards. Control was in the Pay Corps.
The Wellington's bill: tea for three, scones, cakes, a pot of Lapsang. Eleven pounds forty. There's a space at the bottom for a signature.
A sofa, a gas fire, and a cat called Nelson who sleeps on my chest all night. At midnight the goose comes home without the helmet, and with a saveloy.

Stan drops me at the goods yard in a white coat and a flat cap, with forty kippers in the back of the van. "Straight in, straight up, straight out," he says. "If anyone asks, you're my nephew Kevin." Then he goes off for a fry-up.

Down nine flights of stairs, past Sergeant Grimes ("Oi! Kevin!"), out through the goods yard and across the road, with two of Control's grey men behind me, and Control behind them, shouting about his tie.
Down the escalator three steps at a time. Along the platform, through the rush hour. And a train, just pulling in.
